title: Carter's Ceasefire: Four Months of Armed Pause
content:
Jimmy Carter arrived in Bosnia on 18 December 1994, visiting Sarajevo first to meet Izetbegović before traveling to Pale, a former president of the United States acting not as an official envoy but as a private mediator. The timing was not coincidental. The Bihac crisis had brought the war to one of its most dangerous moments — the enclave appeared close to falling, NATO air power had proven insufficient to halt the VRS counteroffensive, and the Western alliance was visibly divided over how to respond. The Contact Group peace plan lay rejected by the Bosnian Serbs. The international diplomatic machinery had stalled. Carter stepped into a vacuum that official channels had failed to fill.

Over several days of shuttle diplomacy between the Bosnian government in Sarajevo, the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale, and intermediaries in Belgrade, Carter negotiated the terms of what became known as the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, or COHA. The agreement called for a complete cessation of hostilities effective 1 January 1995, to last four months. Both sides would hold their current positions. Humanitarian corridors would reopen. Prisoner exchanges would be facilitated. Negotiations toward a permanent settlement would continue.

The agreement was signed on 31 December 1994. On New Year's Day 1995, the guns fell largely silent across Bosnia for the first time in months. The relief was immediate and tangible for civilian populations that had endured sustained combat through the autumn, particularly in the Bihac pocket where the intensity of fighting had brought the enclave to the brink.

Neither side treated the ceasefire as anything other than a pause. The Bosnian government, which had agreed to the COHA under the pressure of the Bihac crisis and with awareness that its forces needed time to reorganize, used the winter months to absorb supplies flowing through newly opened Croatian routes — a consequence of the Washington Agreement signed earlier that year. ARBiH units rotated troops, integrated new equipment, and planned for spring operations. The 5th Corps in Bihac, battered by the November counteroffensive, used the breathing space to reconstitute its depleted formations.

The VRS similarly exploited the ceasefire for military purposes. Ammunition stocks were redistributed. Defensive positions were improved. The logistical pressures created by the Belgrade embargo, while not eliminated, were partially mitigated by four months without major combat consumption. Both sides understood that the ceasefire was a strategic interval, not a step toward peace.

Violations were frequent throughout the four-month period. Sniping continued in Sarajevo. Localized skirmishes flared along front lines in central Bosnia. Neither side's military commanders enforced the ceasefire with the rigour that its terms demanded. UNPROFOR monitored compliance but lacked the mandate or the means to enforce it. The agreement's value lay not in its observance but in the reduction of large-scale offensive operations during a period when weather conditions would have limited them in any case.

Carter's intervention was controversial. Critics argued that the ceasefire rewarded VRS aggression at Bihac by freezing a military situation that favoured the Bosnian Serbs, and that Carter had been manipulated by Karadzic into lending credibility to the Bosnian Serb leadership. Defenders countered that any reduction in killing was worthwhile and that the alternative — continued fighting through the winter with no prospect of resolution — served no one.

The COHA expired on 1 May 1995. Within weeks, the war resumed at an intensity that would surpass anything seen in 1994. The spring and summer of 1995 brought the fall of the eastern enclaves, the second Markale massacre, Operation Deliberate Force, and ultimately the military and diplomatic endgame at Dayton. The Carter ceasefire, in retrospect, was the last pause before the war's final and most violent chapter.
